edges.mechanism: A force requires both magnitude and direction.
edges.effect: Force cannot be fully specified by a scalar magnitude alone.

edges.mechanism: A net force changes an object's momentum and, for constant mass, its velocity.
edges.effect: Changes motion through momentum; for constant mass produces acceleration.
edges.inverse_or_converse: Zero net force permits constant velocity.

edges.mechanism: For constant mass, force determines acceleration through F=ma.
edges.effect: Acceleration is proportional to net force and inversely proportional to mass.

edges.mechanism: Net force is the rate of change of momentum.
edges.effect: Force quantifies how rapidly momentum changes.
edges.inverse_or_converse: Momentum change is time-integral of force.

edges.mechanism: Net force is the vector sum of simultaneously acting forces.
edges.effect: Individual forces combine into one resultant.

edges.mechanism: Only the vector resultant determines translational acceleration in Newtonian mechanics.
edges.effect: Opposing forces can cancel without eliminating individual interactions.

edges.mechanism: For fixed net force, larger mass gives smaller acceleration.
edges.effect: Acceleration is inversely proportional to mass.

edges.mechanism: A nonzero resultant force changes momentum over time.
edges.effect: Momentum evolves in the direction determined by net force.

edges.mechanism: Vector cancellation yields zero resultant force.
edges.effect: No translational acceleration.

edges.mechanism: Translational equilibrium requires zero resultant force.
edges.conditions: Point particle; extended body also needs zero torque.
edges.effect: Acceleration is zero in an inertial frame.

edges.mechanism: Extended-body equilibrium additionally requires zero net torque.
edges.effect: No angular acceleration.

edges.mechanism: An object maintains rest or uniform straight-line motion absent net force.
edges.effect: Motion does not require a sustaining force.

edges.mechanism: Second law is fundamentally a momentum-rate relation.
edges.effect: Provides quantitative dynamics.

edges.mechanism: With constant mass, dp/dt becomes ma.

edges.mechanism: Mutual interaction produces equal and opposite forces.
edges.effect: Forces act on different bodies.

edges.mechanism: Internal forces cancel pairwise in a closed system.

edges.effect: Total momentum remains constant.

edges.mechanism: Net external force accelerates a system's center of mass.
edges.effect: Center-of-mass motion reflects external forcing.

edges.mechanism: Inferring force from acceleration is valid in an inertial frame.
edges.effect: Frame choice affects whether apparent accelerations require real forces.

edges.mechanism: Force addition follows vector algebra.

source_claims.statement: Force is an action capable of changing velocity, shape, resisting other forces, or changing fluid pressure.
Force is a vector because both magnitude and direction matter.
The SI unit of force is the newton, kg·m·s⁻².
Force is central to all three Newtonian laws.
Modern physics replaces the classical force picture with fundamental interactions at the deepest level, while classical force remains practically useful.
Aristotelian physics incorrectly treated continuing force as necessary for continued motion.
Galileo demonstrated that bodies accelerate under gravity independently of mass and retain velocity unless acted on by a force such as friction.
Newton published the three laws of motion in the Principia in 1687.
Newton's second law states that net force is the rate of change of momentum.
For constant mass, acceleration is proportional to net force and inversely proportional to mass.
Newton's third law makes forces mutual interactions between different bodies.
In a closed system internal forces cancel and center-of-mass acceleration is controlled by external force.
Inferring force from acceleration is meaningful in an inertial reference frame.
Forces are additive vector quantities.
Free-body diagrams track forces acting on a selected system.
Equilibrium requires zero resultant force; extended bodies additionally require zero net torque.
Static equilibrium has no acceleration and dynamic equilibrium can involve constant-velocity motion.
Gravitational force follows an inverse-square Newtonian law.
Cavendish measured G in 1798 using a torsion balance.
Newtonian gravity was powerful enough to predict planetary motion and helped predict Neptune through perturbation analysis.
The Lorentz force is q(E+v×B).
Static friction adjusts up to μ_sN and kinetic friction is μ_kN.
Hooke's law gives F=-kΔx for an ideal spring.
Centripetal force is the net inward force required for uniform circular motion.
Continuum mechanics connects force density to pressure gradients, drag and stress.
Torque is r×F and τ=Iα for rigid-body rotation.
Yank is the derivative of force with respect to time.
Impulse is the time integral of force and equals change in momentum.
Work is the line integral of force along displacement and equals change in kinetic energy for net work.
Power is F·v.
Conservative force equals the negative gradient of potential energy.
Conservative forces conserve mechanical energy in a closed system; nonconservative forces transform mechanical energy and are associated with entropy increase.
Force units include newtons, dynes, pound-force, poundals and kilogram-force.
Relativity retains F=dp/dt but redefines momentum as γm0v.
At high velocity, the relation between force and acceleration becomes component-dependent through γ.
F=ma is recovered as a low-velocity approximation when γ≈1.
Four-force satisfies Fμ=mAμ in relativistic mechanics.
Quantum mechanics generally describes microscopic interactions in terms of energy, measurement and probabilities rather than classical forces.
Ehrenfest's theorem connects quantum expectation-value evolution to Newton-like force equations only approximately.
Uncertainty and Pauli exclusion constrain microscopic matter and can produce degeneracy pressure and stability.
Quantum field theory treats force as arising from momentum exchange and field interactions, making fundamental interactions more basic than classical force.
Feynman diagrams represent interactions through vertices and exchanged gauge bosons.
Four fundamental interactions are identified: gravitational, weak, electromagnetic and strong.
Friction and spring forces are macroscopic manifestations of electromagnetic interaction.
Centrifugal force is a pseudo-force associated with accelerating rotating frames.
Newtonian gravity's action-at-a-distance picture conflicts with special-relativistic causal limits.
General relativity reinterprets gravity as inertial motion in curved spacetime rather than a Newtonian force.
The strong interaction acts on quarks/gluons and has a residual nuclear manifestation between hadrons.
Color confinement explains the absence of freely observed quarks.
The weak interaction is mediated by W and Z bosons and produces beta decay.
Electroweak theory unifies electromagnetic and weak interactions at sufficiently high energies/temperatures.

semantic_distinctions.difference: Force is a dynamical cause/interaction quantity; acceleration is the kinematic response. F=ma only under constant-mass Newtonian inertial-frame conditions.
Several forces may act while only their vector sum determines translational acceleration.
Force is dp/dt; momentum change is the time integral of force.
Zero net force does not imply zero individual forces.
Third-law forces act on different bodies; balanced forces cancel on the same selected system.
Mass is inertia/property; weight is gravitational force and varies with gravitational field.
Centripetal describes a required inward net-force role, not a new interaction.
Centrifugal force is frame-dependent and appears in rotating frames.
Normal force is a contact reaction; gravity is a long-range interaction.
Static friction adapts up to a limit without sliding; kinetic friction acts during sliding.
Conservative forces admit a potential and path-independent work; macroscopic dissipative forces generally do not.
Work is energy transfer; power is the rate of that transfer.
Impulse integrates force over time; force is the instantaneous momentum-change rate.
Torque is the rotational analogue determined by force and lever arm.
Relativity retains momentum-rate dynamics but changes the momentum-velocity relation.
Microscopic theory emphasizes fields, amplitudes, observables and momentum exchange rather than classical trajectories.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Gravity as force vs gravity as geometry
semantic_distinctions.difference: GR interprets free fall geometrically as inertial motion in curved spacetime.
Modern field theory treats interactions and conservation laws as more fundamental than classical force language.

W± exchange versus Z0 exchange.
Force is an interaction quantity; stress describes distributed internal force per area.
Pressure is force per area / continuum field; pressure gradients produce distributed force density.

misconceptions.misconception: Force is required to keep an object moving at constant velocity.
misconceptions.correction: In an inertial frame, zero net force permits constant velocity; force changes momentum.

misconceptions.misconception: Acceleration means a force must be present in every reference frame.
misconceptions.correction: Newtonian force inference from acceleration assumes an inertial frame; non-inertial frames require pseudo-force bookkeeping.

misconceptions.misconception: If net force is zero, no forces are acting.
misconceptions.correction: Balanced forces can be nonzero individually while summing to zero.

misconceptions.misconception: Newton's third-law pair cancels the forces on one object.
misconceptions.correction: Third-law forces act on different bodies; cancellation occurs only when considering the combined closed system.

misconceptions.misconception: F=ma is the most fundamental statement of Newton's second law.
misconceptions.correction: F=dp/dt is the general Newtonian statement; F=ma is the constant-mass form.

misconceptions.misconception: Centripetal force is a fifth fundamental force.
misconceptions.correction: Centripetal describes the role of an inward net force; gravity, tension, friction or other interactions can provide it.

misconceptions.misconception: Centrifugal force is a fundamental outward force.
misconceptions.correction: It is a pseudo-force associated with rotating reference frames.

misconceptions.misconception: Mass and weight are the same quantity.
misconceptions.correction: Mass measures inertia; weight is gravitational force.

misconceptions.misconception: All friction is a fundamental interaction.
misconceptions.correction: Macroscopic friction emerges from electromagnetic interactions among matter.

misconceptions.misconception: Conservative force means force is always constant.
misconceptions.correction: Conservative refers to path-independent work and existence of a potential, not constant magnitude.

misconceptions.misconception: Work and power are interchangeable terms.
misconceptions.correction: Work is energy transfer; power is work per unit time.

misconceptions.misconception: Newtonian gravity is exactly correct at all scales and precision.
misconceptions.correction: General relativity corrects Newtonian gravity in regimes where relativistic effects matter.

misconceptions.misconception: Relativity simply changes F=ma to a new scalar equation.
misconceptions.correction: Relativity retains F=dp/dt but changes momentum and produces direction-dependent force/acceleration relations.

misconceptions.misconception: Quantum mechanics is just classical force laws applied to smaller objects.
misconceptions.correction: Quantum mechanics changes the conceptual framework and generally describes interactions through quantum states, probabilities and observables.

misconceptions.misconception: The strong force and nuclear force are exactly synonymous.
misconceptions.correction: The source distinguishes fundamental QCD strong interaction from its residual hadronic/nuclear manifestation.

misconceptions.misconception: The weak force is weak because it has no important physical effects.
misconceptions.correction: It produces beta decay and radioactivity and participates in electroweak unification.

questions.question: Exactly how does force produce acceleration?
questions.answer_focus: Trace net force → dp/dt → m dv/dt → acceleration, including constant-mass and inertial-frame assumptions.

questions.question: Why does force depend on momentum rather than acceleration in the general statement?
questions.answer_focus: Momentum-rate form remains valid when mass or relativistic momentum changes.

questions.question: How can multiple forces produce no acceleration?
questions.answer_focus: Vector cancellation can make net force zero despite nonzero individual forces.

questions.question: Why do action-reaction forces not cancel an object's acceleration?
How does gravity produce acceleration without mass-dependent free-fall acceleration?
questions.answer_focus: F_g scales with test mass while a=F/m, causing test-mass cancellation in Newtonian gravity.

questions.question: What is the relationship among force, impulse and momentum?
questions.answer_focus: Impulse is the time integral of force and equals momentum change.

questions.question: What is the relationship among force, work, energy and power?
questions.answer_focus: Work integrates force over displacement, changes kinetic energy, and power is work rate.

questions.question: How does a potential encode a conservative force?
questions.answer_focus: The negative gradient of potential energy gives force.

questions.question: Why is torque a rotational analogue of force?
questions.answer_focus: Torque is r×F and changes angular momentum/angular velocity.

questions.question: Why does F=ma fail as a general relativistic formula?
questions.answer_focus: Relativistic momentum is γm0v and force-acceleration coupling becomes component-dependent.

questions.question: How does GR change the meaning of gravitational force?
questions.answer_focus: Free fall becomes inertial motion through curved spacetime rather than a Newtonian force.

questions.question: How does quantum theory connect back to classical force?
questions.answer_focus: Ehrenfest's theorem provides an approximate expectation-value correspondence.

questions.question: How do macroscopic forces emerge from fundamental interactions?
questions.answer_focus: Friction and spring forces are described as manifestations of electromagnetic interactions; other macroscopic forces emerge from microscopic physics.

questions.question: What distinguishes the strong interaction from residual nuclear force?
questions.answer_focus: QCD acts on quarks/gluons; residual interaction acts between composite hadrons.

questions.question: How are weak interactions divided into charged and neutral currents?
How does a pressure gradient become a force in a fluid?
questions.answer_focus: Force density is the negative pressure gradient.

questions.question: Why can a force be zero while torque is nonzero?
questions.answer_focus: Forces can cancel translationally while their lines of action produce a net moment.

questions.question: What does the force unit tell us physically?
questions.answer_focus: A newton corresponds to accelerating one kilogram at one meter per second squared.
